1.open: Tell about a time you were at a party or event that was a lot bigger or fancier than you expected. What stood out?
questions: Verse 4 says the king displayed "the glorious riches of his kingdom and the magnificent splendor of his greatness" for 180 days. Why do you think powerful people so often want to show off? What do we do in our own lives that is like this?
In verse 8 the king says there is "no limit" on the drinking, and in verse 10 his "heart was merry with wine" when he gave the order about Vashti. How does the setting help explain what happens next?
In verse 11 the king wants Vashti brought out "to display her beauty to the people and officials." How do you think she was being treated, and what might it have cost her to say no?
Verse 12 says "Queen Vashti, however, refused to come." The text never tells us why. What reasons can you imagine, and how does the silence shape the way you read her?

Memucan says one refusal will cause all women to "despise their husbands" (v. 17). Why might a fearful person turn one small event into a huge threat? When have you seen that happen at work, at home or in a church?

Verse 22 says the king sent letters in every language "proclaiming that every man should be master of his own household." Why might a decree like that fail to produce real respect? What does lasting respect actually grow from?
Christians read Vashti differently. Some see a woman of dignity refusing to be put on display, and others see a wife defying her husband. Where do you land, or where are you unsure, and why?

God is never named in this chapter, yet the story moves on toward Esther. If you have ever felt that God was quiet in your own life, what has that been like for you? You can answer honestly, even if the answer is that you are not sure.
1.life: This week, notice one moment when you feel the urge to control a situation or a person, or to prove how important you are. Pause, and ask God to show you what you are afraid of in that moment.
1.prayer: Thank God that he is not like Xerxes, needing to impress us or force our respect. Ask him to help you trust him in the places where he feels quiet, and to care for anyone in the group who feels overlooked or pressured.
1.tip: Vashti's story can pull the group into a heated debate about marriage and gender roles. Say plainly at the start that Christians read her differently and that the text does not explain her reasons. Keep the focus on what the chapter shows about pride, fear and misused power, and invite people to share without needing to agree.

2.open: Have you ever ended up somewhere you never planned to be? What was it like at first?
questions: The women were gathered by royal order, not invited (vv. 3, 8). How does it change the way you read this story to remember they had no real choice?
Esther was an orphan, and Mordecai "had taken her as his own daughter" (v. 7). Who has played a parent-like or mentor role in your life, and what did they give you?
Esther "did not reveal her people or her lineage" because Mordecai told her not to (v. 10). Why might someone keep part of their identity quiet, and when might that be wise or costly?
Every day Mordecai "would walk back and forth in front of the court of the harem" (v. 11). What does that show about how he cared for her, and how can we show up for people we cannot fully reach?

Esther "found favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her" (v. 15), and the king "loved Esther more than all the other women" (v. 17). What do you make of favor like this, and how might it feel from the inside for her?

God is never named in this chapter, yet Esther becomes queen and Mordecai's deed is recorded (v. 23). Christians read that differently: some see God's hidden hand, others a human story of surviving inside an unjust system. Where do you land, or are you unsure?
Mordecai told Esther about the plot, and she "informed the king on Mordecai's behalf" (v. 22). Why might it matter that a good deed was done quietly and written down for later?
Think of a time you had very little control over what happened to you. How did you get through it, and where, if anywhere, did you sense God, or his absence?
2.life: Think of someone who feels stuck in circumstances they did not choose. This week, do one small thing like Mordecai's daily walk: check in, listen without fixing, and let them know you are there.
2.prayer: Ask God to be near anyone who feels powerless or unseen, including people in the group. Thank him for the people who have looked out for you, and ask for help to do the same for others.
2.tip: Verses 1 to 18 can bring up strong feelings about women being taken and treated as prizes. Don't rush to defend or praise Esther's choices. Name plainly that she had little power, let people say what troubles them, and keep returning to what the text actually says.

3.open: Tell about a time you stuck with something even though everyone around you was doing it differently. It can be as small as a food, a team or a habit.
questions: The royal servants asked Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the command of the king?" (v. 3). They kept at it "day after day" (v. 4). What does it take to hold your ground when people keep pressing you?

The text says only that Mordecai "had told them he was a Jew" (v. 4), and never gives his full reason. What reasons might a person have for refusing to bow, and why do you think the writer left it open?
Christians disagree about Mordecai. Some see faithful obedience to God, others see stubborn pride that put his people at risk. Which of those do you find easier to understand, and why?
Haman "was filled with rage" (v. 5), and one insult grew into a plan to "destroy all of Mordecai's people" (v. 6). How does a small hurt grow into something bigger in a person, or in a group?

In verse 8 Haman describes the Jews as a people whose "laws are different from everyone else's." He never names them. How do people today talk about a group in a way that makes them easier to dislike or ignore?
The king gave away his signet ring and said, "Keep your money" (v. 11), and asked no questions. What does this tell us about what happens when people with power stop paying attention?
The chapter ends with the king and Haman sitting down to drink while "the city of Susa was in confusion" (v. 15). Where do you see people today who are comfortable while others are afraid?
God is never mentioned in this chapter. Have you ever gone through a time when God felt absent or quiet? What was that like, and what would you say honestly about it tonight?
3.life: This week, notice one moment when you are tempted to go along with a joke, a rumor or a put-down about a person or group. Quietly decline to join in, or ask God for courage to do so.
3.prayer: Ask God to protect people who are targeted because of who they are. Ask for courage to stand apart from the crowd when it matters, and for honesty to bring our doubts and fears to him.
3.tip: Someone may want to make Mordecai a clear hero or a clear fool. Say plainly that Christians read him both ways and that the text does not give his reason, then steer the group back to the questions about Haman's rage and the king's silence. Also be gentle with verse 13, which is hard to hear, and let people react to it without rushing to a lesson.

4.open: Think of a time someone asked you for a favor that was bigger than you wanted to give. How did you respond?
questions: Mordecai "wailing loudly and bitterly" in the middle of the city (v. 1) and Jews across the empire fasting and weeping (v. 3). What does this chapter show us about how to respond when bad news is real? When have you let grief show openly, and when have you hidden it?
Esther's first move is to send Mordecai clothes (v. 4). Why might we try to fix how a problem looks before we face the problem itself?

Esther says that anyone who approaches the king uninvited faces death, and that she has not been summoned "for the past thirty days" (v. 11). What fears might be sitting behind her words, beyond the law itself?

Mordecai warns her, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you alone will escape" (v. 13). Where are we tempted to think our comfort or position will keep us safe from what others are facing?

Mordecai asks, "who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (v. 14). Notice he says "who knows" and does not claim to be certain. What do you make of that? How do you tell the difference between a calling and a coincidence?

Mordecai says help "will arise from another place" (v. 14). Some readers hear a quiet reference to God, and others hear simple confidence that someone else would step in. Which way do you lean, and why might it matter either way?
Esther asks the community to fast with her for three days before she acts (v. 16). Who do you turn to when you face something frightening, and what would it look like to ask them to stand with you?

Esther says, "if I perish, I perish!" (v. 16). If you are unsure whether you have that kind of courage, or unsure about God at all, what honestly feels like the hardest part of stepping out when it could cost you?
4.life: Think of one situation where you have stayed silent when you could help someone. Ask one trusted person to pray with you about it this week, then take one small step, such as a phone call, a kind word or an offer of help.
4.prayer: Ask God for honesty about where fear is keeping you quiet. Pray for courage to speak or act for someone who needs it, and for friends to stand beside you.
4.tip: Verse 14 is often used as a slogan, as if every hard moment proves a person was meant to do some great thing. Gently point out that Mordecai asks a question and does not announce a certainty, and that Esther acts with fear, fasting and the support of others. If someone says they feel too afraid to be an Esther, let that stand as an honest answer and invite the group to listen.

5.open: Think of a time you had to ask someone for something that made you nervous. How did you get yourself ready?
questions: Esther goes to the king without being summoned, which could have cost her life. Verse 1 says she "put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court." What do you notice about the way she approaches this moment?
In verse 2 the king sees her and "she found favor in his sight," and he holds out the gold scepter. What do you think she felt in the seconds before that happened?
The king offers her "up to half the kingdom" (v. 3), but she only asks for a dinner (v. 4). Why do you think she holds back her real request? The text does not say, so what are some possible reasons?
Esther invites the king and Haman to a second banquet instead of speaking up (v. 8). Have you ever waited before saying something important? What did waiting do for you, or cost you?
Haman leaves "full of joy and glad of heart" (v. 9), but one man not standing for him fills him with rage. Why can one small thing spoil so much for us?
Haman lists his wealth, his sons and his promotions, then says, "none of this satisfies me" (v. 13). Where do you see that same feeling in our culture, or in your own life?
Zeresh and his friends do not slow him down. They help him build the pole (v. 14). Who speaks into your life when you are angry, and what kind of advice do they give?
Esther's story is full of risk, fear and waiting. If you are in a season where it is hard to see what God is doing, or hard to believe he is, what would you honestly say about that tonight?
5.life: Esther prepared before she acted. This week, pick one hard conversation or decision you have been avoiding. Set aside a few quiet minutes to pray about it and think it through, then take one small step.
5.prayer: Ask God for courage for anyone in the group facing something frightening. Ask him to loosen the grip of envy and pride, and to give us contentment with what we have.
5.tip: God is never named in Esther, so someone may ask where he is in this chapter. Say plainly that Christians read this differently: some see God quietly steering events, others see human courage and chance. Let people share what they see, and do not force an answer.

6.open: Have you ever had a night when you couldn't sleep? What did you end up doing?
questions: The chapter begins with a small detail: "sleep escaped the king" (v. 1). Why do you think the writer starts here? What small, ordinary things have turned out to matter more than you expected?

The record shows Mordecai had exposed a plot against the king, and the king asks, "What honor or dignity has been bestowed on Mordecai for this act?" The answer is, "Nothing has been done for him" (v. 3). How does it feel when good work goes unnoticed? What do you do with that feeling?
Haman has come to ask for Mordecai's death at the very moment the king is thinking about honoring him (v. 4). What stands out to you about the timing?
Haman thinks, "Whom would the king be delighted to honor more than me?" (v. 6). What does his answer in verses 7 to 9 tell us about what he wants most?

The king says, "Do not neglect anything that you have suggested" (v. 10). Haman then leads Mordecai through the city, calling out the honor himself (v. 11). What do you imagine was going through each man's mind?
Mordecai "returned to the king's gate" (v. 12), back to his ordinary post, while Haman rushed home with his head covered. What does the contrast between the two men say to you?
Haman's wife and advisers say, "You will not prevail against him" (v. 13). Why might people who were close to Haman give him this warning now, and not earlier?

God is never named in this book, yet this chapter feels full of well timed events. If you are honest, do you tend to see God behind things like this, or do you find it hard to tell? What makes it easier or harder?
6.life: This week, quietly notice and thank one person whose good work usually goes unseen, at home, work, school or church. Also, when you catch yourself wanting credit, pause and talk to God about it.
6.prayer: Thank God that he sees what no one else notices. Ask for a heart that can serve without needing applause, and for trust when events feel out of your control.
6.tip: The question about whether God is behind the timing is the hard spot, since the book never mentions him and Christians read it differently. Say that plainly, let people answer honestly including those who are unsure, and don't push the group toward one conclusion.

7.open: Have you ever had to speak up about something you were nervous to say out loud? How did it go?
questions: The king asks Esther for the third time what she wants, offering "Even up to half the kingdom" (v. 2). Why do you think Esther waited until now to answer?

Esther asks the king to "grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request" (v. 3). What does it cost her to say this, and what does she risk by putting herself on the same side as her people?
Esther says her people have been "sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation" (v. 4). Why might it matter that she names the danger so plainly instead of hinting at it?

The king asks, "Who is this, and where is the one who would devise such a scheme?" (v. 5). Yet he had approved the decree himself. What does that show about how easily people can sign off on harm without asking who gets hurt?
Esther points straight at "this wicked man" who is sitting right there (v. 6). When have you seen someone find the courage to name a wrong plainly, or wished you had?

Haman dies on the gallows he "had prepared for Mordecai" (v. 10). When someone falls into the trap they set for others, does it feel like justice to you, or like something else? Be honest, even if the answer is mixed.

God is never mentioned in this chapter, yet the timing seems remarkable. Where have you looked back on a hard season and wondered whether God was at work, even though you could not see him then? And where do you still find it hard to tell?
7.life: Think of one situation where you have stayed silent when you could speak, whether it is standing up for someone, telling the truth, or asking for help. This week, take one small, wise step toward speaking, and pray for courage first.
7.prayer: Thank God for people who speak up for others at real cost. Ask for courage and wisdom to speak when it matters, and for trust when God's hand is hard to see.
7.tip: The ending is violent, and some people will cheer while others feel uneasy. Make room for both reactions. Keep the focus on Esther's courage and the reversal of the plot, and avoid turning the discussion into a debate about punishment or about who our own 'Hamans' are. Verse 4 is also unclear in Hebrew, so if someone asks, say translations differ and move on.

8.open: Think of a time something you couldn't undo went wrong. What did you do next?
questions: Haman is dead, but his order still stands. Why do you think the story keeps going instead of ending with his hanging? What does that tell us about how some problems work?
In verse 3 Esther "fell at his feet weeping" for her people, even though she herself was safe. What does it take for someone to keep pleading for others when they could simply rest?
In verse 6 she asks, "How could I bear to see the disaster that would befall my people?" Who is someone you could not bear to watch suffer, and what has that moved you to do?

Verse 8 says a decree "cannot be revoked," so the king's answer is a second decree rather than a cancellation. When something harmful cannot be undone, what does it look like to limit the damage? Where have you seen that done well?

Verse 9 says the message went out "to every people in their own language." Why might it matter that the good news reached people in words they could understand? How does that connect to how we talk about faith?

Verse 11 allows the Jews "to assemble and defend themselves," but also to "destroy, kill, and annihilate." Christians read this differently: some see rightful self-defense, others see vengeance the story reports without approving. How do you read it, and what makes it hard?
Verse 16 says it was "a time of light and gladness, of joy and honor" for the Jews. Think about a time when fear turned into relief for you. What was that like, and how did you respond?
God is never named in this chapter, yet things turn around. If you find it hard to see God at work in a story or in your own life, what would you honestly say about that tonight?
8.life: Think of one person or group who has little voice or protection, and take one small step for them this week. It could be a phone call, a note, a donation, or speaking up for them where they are not in the room.
8.prayer: Thank God for the people who speak up for others at a cost to themselves. Ask for eyes to see who needs a voice, and for honesty about the times when God seems hidden.
8.tip: Verse 11 will likely stir strong reactions. Say plainly at the start that Christians disagree about how to read it, let people share without pressing for one answer, and bring the group back to Esther's care for her people and the relief in verses 16 and 17.

9.open: What is a celebration or tradition in your family that has a story behind it?
questions: Verse 1 says the enemies of the Jews "had hoped to overpower them, but their plan was overturned." Can you think of a time when something feared or planned against you turned out very differently?

Verse 3 says officials helped the Jews "because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them." What does it tell us that help came through a person's power and standing at court? Where do you see God working through ordinary influence today?
The chapter is blunt about the killing, and verse 5 says the Jews "did as they pleased to those who hated them." How do you react to reading this in the Bible?
Three times we are told they "did not lay a hand on the plunder" (vv. 10, 15, 16). Many readers see this as a sign they wanted to survive, not to profit. What do you make of that detail?

In verse 13 Esther asks for another day of fighting and for Haman's sons to be hanged. Some readers think this was needed for safety, others think it went too far. What do you think, and what makes it hard to say?

Verse 22 describes the month "in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday." Is there something in your life you would like to see turned that way? Or is it hard to imagine right now?
Purim includes feasting, gifts to friends and gifts "to the poor" (v. 22). Why might it matter that remembering is done together and includes generosity?
Verse 28 says these days should be remembered "by every generation, family, province, and city." What stories of rescue or faithfulness do you want to pass on, and how could you do it?
9.life: Choose one hard season that has passed, in your life or your family's, and mark it by telling the story to someone else. Include one simple act of generosity, such as sharing a meal or giving a gift to someone in need.
9.prayer: Thank God for the times he has turned sorrow into joy. Ask for honesty about the parts of the story that are hard to read, and for mercy toward people who suffer from violence today.
9.tip: The killing in this chapter will unsettle some people, and others may want to explain it away quickly. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether the text approves of the violence or just reports it. Let people say that it troubles them, and keep returning to what the chapter clearly shows: a people facing destruction who survived, and who chose to remember with joy and generosity.

10.open: Who is someone in your life who had some authority over you and used it well? What did they do?
questions: Verse 1 says King Xerxes "imposed tribute throughout the land, even to its farthest shores." Why might the writer begin the last chapter by reminding us how big and powerful the empire was?
Verse 2 points readers to the royal records of "Media and Persia" for the full story. What does it say about a person's life that most of it ends up in records no one reads anymore?
Verse 3 calls Mordecai "second only to King Xerxes." Think back to how he started in the story. What stands out to you about where he ended up?
Mordecai was "highly favored by his many kinsmen" (v. 3). What do you think it takes for someone with power to be liked and trusted by their own people, not just feared?
Verse 3 says he was "seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen." What would that look like in a workplace, a family, a church or a neighborhood today?

The book of Esther never names God, yet many readers see him quietly at work behind the scenes. Others see mostly human courage and loyalty. Where have you seen things work out in your own life, and how do you tell the difference between luck, effort and God?
Some of us feel we have very little influence. Where do you have a little power, even a small amount, to do good for someone else this week?
If you are honest, does a happy ending like this one feel believable to you, or does it feel distant from your own experience? Why?
10.life: Pick one place where you have some say, like your home, your job, a team or a group of friends. This week, do one thing there that helps someone else rather than yourself, and do it quietly.
10.prayer: Ask God to help each person use whatever influence they have for the good of others. Pray also for anyone in the group who feels overlooked or unsure whether God is at work in their life.
10.tip: Verse 3 can sound like a tidy happy ending, and someone may point out that real life often does not end that way. Let that honest reaction stand. Gently note that the chapter praises how Mordecai used his position, and that the book's silence about God is something Christians read in different ways.
